msDesc.head: A Persianate South Asian album of portraits of Mughal and Hindu holy persons, rulers, and nobles, and Persian calligraphy specimens.

msContents.summary: This Persianate South Asian album of forty folios preserves thirty-eight paintings and drawings, and several Persian calligraphy specimens. All folios bear the seal impression of Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809), who served as Chief Justice in Calcutta between 1774 to 1783, during which time, he amassed a considerable collection of manuscripts, drawings, and antiquarian objects. Many also bear the name of a former owner named Nawāb Muẓaffar Jang

seal.p:
Rectangular seal impressions, intaglio carved in nasta‘līq script in two stacked lines, double-ruled, of former owner Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809), dated 1775, along with a regnal year 16 of George III, King of Great Britain (b. 1738, r. 1760–1820) reads from bottom upwards:
سر ایلاجه ایمپی چیف جستس سنه ۱۶، ۱۷۷۵
(Sir Īlāhah Īmpī Chīf Justis, sanah 16, 1775).
Dimensions:
19 26

history.origin: The content originates from different periods and sources, formed into an album either assembled for, or acquired by, Nawāb Muẓaffar Jang, the honorific title of Nawāb Muʿīn al-Dawlah Mubāriz al-Mulk Khānkhānān Sayyid Muḥammad Riz̤āʾ Khān Bahādur Muẓaffar Jang (ca. 1717–1792 CE) the Nāʾib Nāẓim (Deputy Governor) of Bengal and Bihar, in Calcutta (Kolkata). Acquitted of charges brought by brought by Warren Hastings of mismanaging funds during the Bengal Famine of 1769, the long, nearly two-year trial ruined his finances and forced him to lease his Calcutta home to the East India Company. Those circumstances apparently forced him to sell a portion of his renowned collection before his death in Murshidabad in 1792.

provenance.p: Probably sold by Sayyid Muḥammad Riz̤āʾ Khān to Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809), as per the latter's seal impressions. Impey served as the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William between 1774 to 1783, where he amassed a considerable collection, before he returned to Britain and passed away.

The London firm of Harry Phillips (d. 1840) sold Impey's collection 21 May 1810, of which Nº 355 containing forty portraits of great personnges and allegorical subjects, splendidly illuminated may possibly be this volume, acquired by an unidentified buyer.
Subsequently acquired from an unidentified source by scholar Nathaniel Bland (1803–1865) for his library at Randalls Park, Leatherhead.

After Bland's death, London bookseller Bernard Quaritch (1819–1899) sold his oriental manuscripts to Alexander Lindsay, 25th Earl of Crawford (1812–1880) in June, 1866, paid in two instalments of £450 and £400, and then moved to Bibliotheca Lindesiana at Haigh Hall, Wigan.
Purchased by Enriqueta Rylands (1843–1908) in 1901 from James Ludovic Lindsay, 26th Earl of Crawford (1847–1913).

acquisition.p: Bequeathed by Enriqueta Rylands (1843–1908) in 1908 to the John Rylands Library, Manchester.

source.p: Bibliographical description based on a manuscript catalogue by Michael Kerney, circa 1890s.
Manuscript description by Jake Benson in 2026 with reference to the volume in hand.

msContents.summary: This calligraphy specimen primarily features an unidentified Persian mas̱navī (couplet) poem. The style of suggests it may possibly be from the Safavid Empire in circa the 16th to 17th centuries CE.

msItem.title: Mas̱navī
msItem.author: Anonymous
msItem.quote: درین ره خضر همت همرهم بس * حریم نیستی منزلگهم بس | حریف کنج خلوتخانه فقر * دل هشیار و جان آگهم بس | چرا منت کشم بهر چراغی * فروغ مجلس از شمع مهم بس | مرا گر دولت شاهنشهی نیست * جگربسته درون خون ته تهم بس | ز بیرون گر لباس تو به تو نیست * فراغ از دولت شاهنشهم بس | چو جامی گر نه کوتاه آستینم * ز مشت سفله دست کوتهم بس
فریاد برآمد که گرفتاری چند * در زلف تو ای برده دلِ رازی چند | پرسیدم از نشان که گیاهند شما * دل‌ها دیدم بسته به هر تاری چند

msContents.summary: Profile portrait of Rajah of Benares (Varanasi), Chayt Singh (r. 1770–1781, d. 1810), seated on a veranda outdoors under a canopy, facing left, smokes a waterpipe while an attendant behind him, to his right, fans him with a morchal made of peacock feature.

figure.figDesc: Portrait of Chayt Singh (r. 1770–1781, d. 1810), who fomented against the East India Company in 1781, in which he captured Warren Hastings. Hastings escaped disguised as a woman, and the plot ultimately failed, so Chayt Sing escaped with his brother to Gwalior and lived out his days there.
